clue.text: Dead good

definitions.meaning: someone who has died has left the earth behind
informal praise for something excellent enough to seem unearthly

explanation.surface: Northern English slang for something really excellent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dead good' is British slang for 'very good', which hides the fact that the two words are separate definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both a euphemism for having departed life and informal praise meaning superb.

clue.text: Such people have very little in common

definitions.text: Such people have very little in common

parts.words: Such people have very little in common
parts.note: read 'in common' as 'all alike' rather than 'shared with each other': these are people who, one and all, own very little

explanation.surface: A group of people who share almost no interests.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests people with no shared interests. Read instead that what these people share is having very little: the poor and disadvantaged.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: the deprived, as a group, own hardly anything and lack advantages.

clue.text: First love I trap in stages

parts.note: love is a score of zero in tennis, which looks like the letter O

indicators.note: in tells you the I and the trap sit inside the word for stages

parts.note: a motor rally is a race run as a series of timed stages
a gin is a snare for catching game

explanation.surface: Someone's earliest romance, which I catch a bit at a time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First love' reads as one phrase but splits: 'First' is the definition and 'love' a tennis zero. 'stages' is the noun: a motor race of this kind is run in stages.
explanation.definitionFit: As adverbs both mean at the outset, as in 'the house was first a chapel'.

clue.text: Simple thing, lifting a doormat

definitions.note: a doormat is a person who meekly lets others walk over them; the clue names the person where the answer is the adjective describing them

indicators.note: in a down clue lifting means the letters are read from the bottom up

parts.note: simple and dim both describe someone slow-witted
it is the pronoun for a thing

explanation.surface: Picking up the mat at the front door is an easy job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lifting' turns DIM and IT together, read upwards as a down entry. The definition is loose: a doormat is a submissive person, where the answer is the adjective for one.
explanation.definitionFit: A doormat is a meek, submissive person, so the noun loosely stands for the adjective describing such a person.

clue.text: Fresh as nice red rose

indicators.note: fresh suggests a new version, so the letters of the three words that follow are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Something as fresh as a lovely red flower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rose' looks like the flower but is the past tense of rise. 'Fresh' is the anagram signal for 'as nice red'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rose is the past tense of rise, and prices that rose went up, a synonym.

clue.text: Shrewd Mayfair lady pulling plug

parts.note: Mayfair is a smart district of London in the W1 postcode, with the 1 written as the letter I

indicators.note: pulling means taking something out, so the plug is withdrawn from the lady

parts.note: taken as written
a plug is a promotional mention, an ad

explanation.surface: A sharp-witted woman from a posh part of London empties the bath.
explanation.walkthrough: Mayfair's London postcode is W1, written WI. 'pulling' removes AD (a plug, as in advertisement) from LADY, leaving LY.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms: both describe someone cunning and sharp in their dealings.

clue.text: Lecturer goes for surprise rave!

indicators.note: to rave is to talk wildly, so the letters of the three words before it are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A university teacher heads off to an unexpected all-night dance party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rave' is the anagram signal for 'goes for surprise'. A Regius Professor holds a university chair founded by a British monarch, mostly at old universities such as Oxford and Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: A holder of a royally founded university chair teaches students, so is an example of an academic who lectures.

clue.text: Leather satisfies people

parts.note: something that does is good enough, as in 'that does nicely'
your kin are your people, your family

explanation.surface: A hide product that keeps customers happy.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a soft hide taken from a female deer, so an example.

clue.text: One letter with another, in a sense

parts.note: A is one letter of the alphabet
cum is Latin for with, used in English in phrases like kitchen-cum-diner
another letter: en is the spelt-out name of the letter N

explanation.surface: Two pieces of post arrive together, in a manner of speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a sense' reads as a hedge, but 'sense' alone is the definition, meaning good judgement. The letters are of the alphabet, not the post.
explanation.definitionFit: Sense here means sound judgement, a synonym for sharp insight.

clue.text: A yellow devil, one nursed by old lady

parts.note: a cad is a scoundrel, a devil in the sense of a wicked fellow

indicators.note: something nursed is held in the arms, so the one is held inside the old lady

parts.note: old lady is slang for one's mother, mum in British English
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: A cowardly demon, cared for by an elderly woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nursed by' puts I inside MUM. The definition works because the metal gives its name to a vivid artists' pigment.
explanation.definitionFit: The metal names a vivid artists' pigment, so it is an example of a shade.

clue.text: City record buried in volcanic hill

indicators.note: something buried lies within, so the record sits inside the hill

parts.note: a cone is the conical hill a volcano builds
a log is a written record

explanation.surface: A town's archives lie under the ash of a volcano.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a German cathedral town on the Rhine, an example.

clue.text: Mother's reminder to change husbands

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother

indicators.note: to change something is to alter it, so the letters of the word before are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A mum prompts her daughter to swap spouses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'husbands' could be a verb, to use sparingly, and 'change' suggests swapping one for another; here it is the plain plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Husbands are by definition wedded males, a plain description.

clue.text: Love means nothing

definitions.meaning: a term of endearment, as love is; this one is heard in the English Midlands
in cricket, a batter's score of zero

explanation.surface: A cynic's view of romance.
explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions joined by 'means': a Midlands term of endearment like 'love', and a cricket score of nought. Love is also zero in tennis, which makes the surface read as a truism.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a British term of endearment and a cricketer's score of zero.

clue.text: Nothing published — we did supply everywhere

parts.note: FA is British slang for nothing, short for sweet Fanny Adams
a newspaper that ran a story published it

indicators.note: supply here is the adverb from supple, in a flexible way, so the two words before it are bent into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: With no new titles out, our firm still delivered stock to every shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supply' looks like the verb to provide but is read as 'in a supple way', the anagram signal making DWIDE from 'we did'. FA is British slang for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for over a large area, in all places.

clue.text: They describe Scottish island's backward hills

indicators.note: backward tells you the island's name runs from its last letter to its first

parts.note: Arran is an island in the Firth of Clyde, off Scotland's west coast
tors are rocky hills, as on Dartmoor in south-west England

explanation.surface: Writers give an account of a Hebridean isle's remote uplands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backward' turns ARRAN, an island off Scotland's west coast, into NARRA.
explanation.definitionFit: Storytellers relate and depict events, which is what describing is.

clue.text: Vehicle may be unstable, so never load rubbish

definitions.note: 'so' means 'in this condition': the answer is the adjective for the condition in which a vehicle may be unstable

indicators.note: rubbish is something in a mess, so the two words before it are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A warning not to pile refuse onto a lorry that could tip over.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole first part: 'so' means 'in this state', the state in which a vehicle may be unstable. 'rubbish' is the anagram signal for 'never load'.
explanation.definitionFit: A lorry carrying too much weight may tip, so the phrase describes that condition.

clue.text: Ski resort area nearly finished

indicators.note: nearly means the word after it stops just short, losing its final letter

parts.note: something spent is used up, finished

explanation.surface: The slopes around a winter sports town are almost completed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nearly' drops the T from SPENT.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a famous Colorado town for winter sports, an example.

clue.text: Cast left in dump

parts.note: hove is a past tense of heave, to throw or cast

explanation.surface: The actors of a play, abandoned in a grotty place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' is not the actors but a verb in the past tense, threw. 'in' just joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal words for a squalid, wretched dwelling.

clue.text: Easy to digest? Not initially eaten by ambassador before a meal

indicators.note: before tells you the first assembly is placed ahead of the a
what is eaten ends up inside the eater, so the shortened word goes within the ambassador

parts.note: HE is His or Her Excellency, the title of an ambassador

indicators.note: not initially means the word loses its opening letter

parts.note: light food is easy to digest

explanation.surface: Something gentle on the stomach wasn't at first touched by the diplomat ahead of dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a British early-evening meal of cooked food served with a pot of tea, eaten in place of a later dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a British early-evening spread of cooked food with a hot drink, an example.

clue.text: Try to stop speaking at any time

parts.note: to end something is to stop it

indicators.note: speaking tells you the phrase after it is heard, not read

parts.note: ever means at any time, as in 'if you ever need help'

explanation.surface: Make an effort never to talk again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'speaking' asks you to say EVER, which sounds like the last six letters of the answer in British pronunciation.
explanation.definitionFit: As verbs both mean to attempt, synonyms.

clue.text: Run one pipe upwards

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run
the Roman numeral for one is I
to pipe is to sing in a high voice, as birds do

explanation.surface: Lay a single length of tube going up the wall.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'upwards' looks like a signal to read something from the bottom; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something heading upwards is ascending or climbing, a synonym.

clue.text: Turn left and head for footpath that's in front of hotel

definitions.note: in the NATO spelling alphabet the word for G comes immediately ahead of Hotel, the word for H

parts.note: a go is a turn in a game

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, here that of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Directions for a walker: go left and make for the path by the inn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head for' takes the F of footpath. The definition is cryptic: in the NATO spelling alphabet this word, for G, comes straight before Hotel, for H.
explanation.definitionFit: In the NATO phonetic alphabet the code word for G directly precedes Hotel, the word for H.

clue.text: Calm detectives entering flat, extremely serious

definitions.note: read as a noun, a state of tranquillity

indicators.note: entering means the detectives go inside the word for flat

parts.note: a plane surface is a flat one
CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, the detective branch of British police

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters, here those of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Unruffled police officers walk into an apartment, looking very grave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calm' is a noun here, not an adjective describing the detectives, who are the plain-clothes branch of British police.
explanation.definitionFit: Calm as a noun means tranquillity, a synonym.

clue.text: They store water through hydrokinetic action

indicators.note: through says the answer runs through the two words that follow, across their join

explanation.surface: Reservoirs hold their contents by harnessing the movement of fluids.
explanation.walkthrough: 'through' is the signal that the answer runs across the join of 'hydrokinetic action'.
explanation.definitionFit: These desert plants hold moisture in their fleshy stems, a description.

clue.text: Amateur orchestra gets further

parts.note: LSO is the London Symphony Orchestra

explanation.surface: A community band makes more progress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets' just joins the pieces to the definition, which is 'further' as in 'further, I should add'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both can introduce an extra point, meaning in addition, synonyms.

clue.text: Took back good little light with switch

definitions.note: read as an adjective: fitted with, or flipped by, a kind of two-position switch

indicators.note: back tells you the word for took is written from its last letter to its first

parts.note: got and took both mean obtained, as in 'I got the last one'
an LED is a small light, a light-emitting diode

explanation.surface: Returned a decent small lamp that came with its own on-off button.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Took back' reads as one phrase, returned, but splits into a word and the signal that turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes something flipped between two states, as a two-position control does.

clue.text: See lips showing red

parts.note: the letter C is pronounced like see, and stands for it in text messages such as CU
the lip of a cup or crater is its rim
a film that is showing is on

explanation.surface: Look at a mouth wearing scarlet lipstick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is the letter C, as in text-message shorthand, and 'showing' is ON, as a film is.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a deep shade of that colour, an example.

clue.text: Production crew die near igneous rocks

indicators.note: to rock is to shake about, so the three words before it are shaken into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A film team perish beside volcanic boulders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rocks' looks like a noun, the volcanic stones, but is a verb here: the anagram signal for 'die near igneous'.
explanation.definitionFit: They are the sound technicians on a recording or broadcast, an example of such a team.
